title: Process Only Where You Look: Hardware and Algorithm Co-optimization for Efficient Gaze-Tracked Foveated Rendering in Virtual Reality
problem: Image rendering in VR head-mounted displays (HMDs) is computationally expensive, particularly for real-time applications where low latency is mandatory. Existing gaze-tracking and foveated rendering approaches impose high algorithmic and hardware costs that compound the overall rendering budget.
motivation: VR HMDs must render high-quality, immersive visuals at low latency on power-constrained embedded SoCs, and leveraging the human visual system's foveal concentration can eliminate unnecessary computation in peripheral regions if gaze can be tracked efficiently.
method: The paper proposes POLONet, an efficient multitask deep learning framework for real-time eye-movement tracking, co-designed with a dedicated POLO accelerator integrated as a plug-in for VR HMD SoCs. The system exploits the observation that human gaze is concentrated in a small foveal region, so full-resolution rendering is performed only where the eye is looking while peripheral regions are rendered at reduced quality. The hardware-algorithm co-optimization jointly minimizes gaze-tracking latency and rendering compute cost through a tightly coupled accelerator-SoC interface.
key_novelty: A hardware-algorithm co-design that unifies multitask gaze tracking (POLONet) with a dedicated SoC accelerator (POLO) to achieve end-to-end foveated rendering with minimal latency overhead.
contributions: POLONet: a multitask deep learning framework for low-latency eye tracking on VR HMDs.
POLO accelerator: a plug-in hardware block for VR HMD SoCs that accelerates gaze-informed foveated rendering.
Algorithm-hardware co-optimization that reduces end-to-end latency by up to 3.9x compared to state-of-the-art gaze tracking methods.
Demonstration of the POLO system integrated into a complete VR rendering pipeline targeting real-time performance.

metrics.speedup: 3.9x reduction in end-to-end latency vs. latest gaze tracking methods

limitations: Specific baseline systems, quantitative energy results, and area metrics are not disclosed in the abstract.
